accuracy.evidence: Checked against the DfE Relationships Education, RSE and Health Education statutory guidance (secondary: respectful relationships, being safe, online and media), the Serious Crime Act 2015 s.76 offence of controlling or coercive behaviour, and the Criminal Justice and Courts Act 2015 and Online Safety Act 2023 on threatening to share intimate images. Childline 0800 1111 and loveisrespect text LOVEIS to 22522 are the published numbers. p2, p4, m7 and m8 are whole positive at every range corner (p4 min 7-6=1).

misconceptions.evidence: Targets documented teen beliefs from the Women's Aid and Childline reports and Barter et al. (2009, NSPCC) on teen partner violence: jealousy as proof of love (step 2 prediction, p3), abuse must be physical (step 3 prediction, challenge 'hit'), kind days cancel control (step 3 feedback, m6, challenge 'cancel'), constant tracking is caring (m10, challenge 'care'), and that confronting a partner or promising secrecy is the right way to help (step 5 feedback, m4).

lab_distinct.evidence: flaghealthy is the only lab that places behaviours on a three-band healthy–unhealthy–abusive spectrum, has the learner find control days within a mixed week so the pattern emerges, and practises assertive boundary replies and safe help choices. flagmirror reflects on your own habits with a slider and goal-setting; flagfriend and flagagree handle friendship and resolving disagreements. The 30% shingle gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner first sorts six green and red flags, then sees that the line is not binary when sulking lands in the middle and threats at the far end, then finds four control days among three kind ones so the idea of coercive control as a pattern is built from their own taps. They then rehearse assertive replies in three situations and choose safe ways to help a friend, with Childline and 999/911 named.

predictions.evidence: Two locked predictions with tempting wrong answers that teens really give: 'Jealousy that stops you seeing friends shows they care' (True, it shows love) and 'To spot coercive control, what matters most?' (One really bad day, or Whether they ever hit). The lab then tests the prediction directly: the sulking card lands in Unhealthy and the week shows the pattern.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions with rotated answer order and a specific explanation for every wrong answer through the why() if-chain: care, normal, once, hit, push and guilt, fight, secret, cancel and sorry, choose and phone, for example 'Control does not have to be physical. Threats, tracking and put-downs count too.' Feedback is announced in an aria-live status line.

readability.evidence: Measured with the validator's FK formula: learner kid text grade 2.9 (target 6.5) and learner adult text grade 6.6 (target 9.5). Kid text uses short sentences and everyday words (red flag, line, pattern, boundary) so the safety message is clear to anxious readers; adult text names the statutory guidance, the 2015 offence and the misconceptions in plain sentences. Lab copy is one line per card.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph has a job: green flags, red flags, the spectrum, coercive control as a pattern, and boundaries and help; the adult side covers the curriculum, the spectrum model, misconceptions and safe help. The content gate's filler patterns passed, and the help numbers appear in the lab, the lesson and the mastery pool.

mobile.evidence: Every canvas tap target has a button twin in the Lab controls group, the week view rotates text so seven days fit a phone width, and the browser gate walked desktop and iPhone 13 with Show me reaching the tick within 6 seconds and the Challenge visible.

accessibility.evidence: axe was clean in light and dark themes on both viewports. The canvas aria-label is updated with each action, buttons carry aria-labels with the full card text, the help line is real text below the lab, and colours come from the theme palette so contrast passes in both themes.

Barter, C. et al. (2009) Partner exploitation and violence in teenage intimate relationships, NSPCC
